questions.question: Trace the chain from self-sufficiency to trade, naming barter's four failures and money's answering functions.
questions.expected_answer: Self-sufficient households consumed only what they made; the agricultural revolution produced surplus, releasing people into specialisation — and specialists must exchange. Barter's failures: the double coincidence of wants (finding someone who has what you want AND wants what you have); indivisibility (half a goat buys nothing); no common measure of value (every pair of goods needs its own ratio); no store of value (perishable surplus rots). Money answers each: a medium of exchange dissolves the double coincidence; divisibility fits any purchase; a unit of account gives one measure — prices; a store of value lets wealth wait. Good moneys were durable, divisible, portable and scarce.

questions.question: Describe the market's evolutionary tracks and the state's three historic entries.
questions.expected_answer: Markets evolved through deepening specialisation (the division of labour multiplying productivity, feeding and fed by markets); expanding trade and transport (each road, ship and railway widening the market's circle); mercantile and commercial law (contracts, weights and measures, courts — trust made institutional as strangers traded); and evolving business forms (sole traders, partnerships, then companies with shares spreading risk and gathering capital), with technological progress threading throughout. The state entered by involving itself in trade (regulation, chartered companies, ports), by taxation (giving rulers a permanent stake in growth), and by financing infrastructure (roads, harbours, railways — expensive, benefiting all, repaying only indirectly: the classic public investment).

questions.question: Explain industrialisation's four components and weigh its consequences, including South Africa's mining route.
questions.expected_answer: Components: manufacturing at factory scale; technological progress (machines embodying knowledge); the mobilisation of energy — the decisive break, replacing muscle with water, steam, electricity and oil; and mechanisation across farming, transport and industry. Consequences: productivity multiplied and goods cheapened; urbanisation as factories gathered workers; new classes — industrial employers and workers — whose conflicts produced labour relations; world markets knitted together; and costs — harsh conditions, child labour, pollution — that summoned labour law. South Africa industrialised through mining: diamonds and gold drew railways inland and concentrated labour under the migrant system, with social costs the country still carries — gains and costs entangled.
